utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber has not decided on the pending application for protective measures and the Chamber would like to give an opportunity to further -- to put further questions to the witness in relation to that before we decide. And, of course, depending on the questions the parties have, the Chamber might want to put some questions to him as well. Therefore, at this moment, we should start in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we wait for a second until all background ground noise ceases. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Sinobad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 7173 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, do you recall being interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on 21 February and 7 March 2007 and providing a written statement to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is that the statement that we see on the screen right now, and is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review the statement before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you have informed us that you wanted to make two small corrections. One is in the translation of paragraph 3, where it says, "Autoprevoz Obrovac," whereas the translation says, "Autoprevoz Otocac." The right one is "Autoprevoz Obrovac." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And the second correction that you wish to make at paragraph 22, on page 4, and you like to remove the word "old" when describing the barracks near the town of Benkovac. So instead of "old facility," it should just say "facility." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now with these two corrections does your statement accurately reflect what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Are the contents of the statement you signed in March 2007, subject to those two corrections, true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Finally, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in 2007, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would like to admit into evidence 65 ter 7173, pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, as we have learned from the Defences at earlier stages. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2362. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would like to read out a short summary of the evidence of the witness contained in his statement that was just admitted into evidence for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Dusan Sinobad was born in the village of Kolarina in the Benkovac municipality and lived in the Benkovac municipality all of his life until Operation Storm. He witnessed the shelling of the municipality on the 4th of August. On that day, he observed shelling in a residential area of the town of Benkovac. He tried to go to his home village of Kolarina, located on the outskirts of the town, but the shelling of his village was so intense he could not go there and had to return. He learned from other residents of villages who came to Benkovac that other villages around Benkovac were also being shelled. As a director of the bus company, he was told to prepare his buses so that civilians could be taken to a safer place. This concludes my summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can give a hard copy of the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, that statement is just for your reference, if I refer to it or if other counsel refer to it, feel free to look at it so that your evidence is as accurate as possible. That statement is now in evidence. I want to discuss a few of the matters that are contained in your statement in a little more detail. And the first issue I want to explore with you is the shelling as you mention in your statement and as I had summarized and my first series of questions is designed to help the Trial Chamber distinguish between what you actually saw and what you heard from other people. My first question is directed at paragraph 15 in your statement. And there you say: "I went to my office at about 6.00 a.m., which was my normal time. On the journey, there, I could see that the shells were falling around the residential areas of the town and not the town centre itself." Now, first of all, when -- can you tell the Court what you mean by the town centre? How large of an area are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards the town itself, if we take into account its size and width, it's about one kilometre. When I say the centre of town, I partially have in mind that the town as a whole. That's to say, between the barracks and the residential quarters of Barice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 5186 on the screen; and if we could have the assistance of the court usher to help the witness mark this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, can you please mark for us where this residential area is where you saw shells falling on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the residential area called Barice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you please an A next to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you know how many shells that you saw land there? How many impacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three to four shells, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was there any damage done to that residential area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The shells landed in front of the apartment buildings which formed part of the area. They landed right in front of them, damaging the building itself. The facade was damaged as well as the window-panes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say you observed this when you were going to the office. Did you observe the actual impacts then or did you observe the result of the impact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was leaving the apartment building, towards the south, I could see the area, and I could still see smoke, and I noticed pieces of shrapnel on the facade. There was still some smoke at the site of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think you had tried to mark -- when you talk about residential buildings, I think your pen just went -- don't write anything, but that's on the -- what is right above letter A right now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Where I drew the line across, that's where the buildings are, just above the letter A. That's where the complex of buildings is. The rest is a meadow. There are no buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say in your statement that there were no shells in the town centre itself but in this residential area, does that mean that this area -- you don't consider this to be the town centre, this Barice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These are residential blocks that had been built several years previously. It was the edge of town, beyond which there were no more buildings, at least that were part of the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could you please now circle and put a letter B next to what you consider -- what you consider to be the centre of the town of Benkovac, which you have mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I draw a circle or just write a letter to mark the centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just mark a circle around whatever you consider to be the centre of the town of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if could you also put a B, maybe above it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have the marked map admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, marked map shall be given Exhibit P2363. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, you also say in your statement that Benkovac had been shelled before the 4th of August. Can you tell the Court the difference between the shelling that had occurred in the past and the shelling on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the shelling of town itself, in the period between 1992 and 1995, there would be shelling of the town two to three times a month, and then only one or two -- on one or two occasions during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how long would that shelling last, in the period between 1992 and 1995, before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That particular shelling would last some 10 to 15 minutes, until the missiles were fired, and then there would be a stop in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to refer to the shelling of your home village that you saw the shelling of Kolarina, and that is referenced for you and for everyone else in paragraphs 18 and 19 of your statement. Can you, first of all, confirm that the village of Kolarina is approximately 6 to 7 kilometres south-east of the town of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 7 kilometres, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see that shelling yourself; or was it something that you were told by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, on the 4th, I was an eye-witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Court what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since shells could be heard throughout that morning in the areas that were normally shelled, at around 11.00 a.m., I tried to work my way to the village, since my father, brother, and sister-in-law, as well as my wife's family were living there at the time. Therefore, at around 11.00 a.m., I got into my car and headed for the village. On the way to the village, on a slope called Vignjina [phoen], I met Major Milos Ostojic who was coming from the direction of my village. I knew him because is he my wife's relative. He pulled over next to my car and said that I should not try and proceed any further because the village had been shelled for the entire morning. I went on, nevertheless, some 7 to 800 metres, just on the entrance to the village, that's Pajo Mizrak's house, next to his house that I stopped. I parked my car behind a wall, by way of some protection for the car. I hurried, running into his house, and, at that precise moment, from the point when I got out of the car and until the point I got into the house, I saw shells falling. I waited there for a while, about half an hour, until there was a lull. I then got into my car and returned to Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. To your knowledge, there were any military positions in the village of Kolarina, any Serb military positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Throughout the war, there had been no military positions in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how far from the village of Kolarina were the closest military positions of the army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 3 and a half kilometres up the -- up the hill called Strazbenica, to the south-east of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also say in your statement, and this time I'm referring to paragraph 23, that you were told by others that their villages were also being shelled and these people were coming into Benkovac. Did you talk to these people yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on my return from the village, I saw that columns of people had the -- by that time started arriving into Benkovac. They were using trucks and whatever vehicles they had. Of course, we were interested in knowing what was going on. These individuals told us that the nearby villages were being shelled and that they simply had to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were these people that you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. It was a small community. We all knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did they tell you whether they were coming to Benkovac as their final destination or whether they were planning to go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the people stayed in Benkovac, and others passed through Benkovac and went on further inland.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So did everyone from these surrounding villages come to Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. For the most part, people arriving in Benkovac were from the villages to the west or to the west -- to the south-west of Benkovac; in other words, the villages in the direction of Biograd and further on in the direction of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just before we move in to another short topic, at paragraph 22 of your statement, you mentioned a military facility. And except for that barracks, was there any other military facility in the town of Benkovac or around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In Benkovac proper, there were none. It was a kilometre or over a kilometre that the Slobodan Macura barracks was located in the direction of Zadar. It had been there since World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were there any units of the army of the RSK stationed in those barracks on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another short topic to address, so perhaps it is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that topic take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Probably ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then would you conclude your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If can you do it in ten minutes perhaps we'd rather continue for another ten minutes and then have the half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have D931 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sinobad, there will be a document that will appear on your screen and it is discussed in your statement. It's a document that you prepared in 1993 and you called it an evacuation plan. I'm going to wait for it appear on the screen and when it appears, I would like you to tell the Court why you had prepared such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's D931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That matter is extensively dealt with in the statement, but if would you please focus on what is new rather than to go through it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, let me instead ask you, as the Presiding Judge has indicated, you have described in your statement what the purpose of this plan was. Do you remember that from your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were you told when you prepared this document or -- where the -- where the buses were to be taken in the case of an emergency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The staff required me to dispose of the buses in such a way that they would be able to cover the entire town in a case of emergency. They did not specify what sort of emergency that would be, or where they were supposed to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can have D253 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, I'm going to show you a document I showed you yesterday. It's the evacuation plan prepared in the municipality of Benkovac. And I will ask you when it comes up on the screen, whether you had seen this document before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So in your statement when you referred to evacuation plan, you're referring to D931, that document that you had prepared. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which I signed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sinobad, when did the people from Benkovac, who had their own modes of transportation, start leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the people arriving from villages and passing through Benkovac was at 4.00 p.m., and then by 8.00 p.m., the columns were already formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just make a correction on the transcript, 32, page 32, line -- oh, it's already done. Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You talked about the people arriving from villages and passing through. I want to focus on the people who lived in Benkovac, those that their had own modes of transportation. If they did, when did they start leaving the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., since at 6.00 p.m., I was summoned to the staff, in the municipal building, where I was required to make sure that all the buses were up and ready, filled up with fuel, in order to transport people away. That's when I approached my associates, my subordinates, told them to do as much, and word got around about it, I suppose, and that's when the whole process of evacuation stepped up -- got stepped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify the timing. In your statement you mention that meeting took place at about 4.00 p.m. Now you said it's about 6.00. Can you clarify for us, if you remember precisely, or give us a range when that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At around 4.00 p.m., I got called to report to the municipality, to the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At paragraph 21 of your statement you say that you were called in the mayor's office and -- actually let me read it to you to make sure it is accurate. "At about 4.00 p.m. I was called to the municipal office by one of the war staff which included the mayor, Stevo Vuksa and his advisors, the president of the municipality, and other prominent officials of the municipality. At that meeting I was ordered to prepare my buses with fuel for the transfer of the civilians to safer areas. There was no explanation as to whether any order had been received for any evacuation. I was further told that if there was not enough fuel for the buses at our station, that I could get fuel from the military barracks." Let me just go to paragraph 26 and then I will ask you my last questions. There you say: "The first bus left at about 7.00 p.m. We had been told at the earlier meeting to head for the interior of the Krajina and that the ultimate destination was to be Bosanski Petrovac, as this was the only direction that we could take to avoid the Croatian forces. The instructions that I received at the 4.00 p.m. meeting was that the population should return on those buses when the situation had settled down." Now, first of all, is that accurate, what I read out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sinobad, were you told anything by the mayor or the others present at this meeting as to why such a decision had been taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told anything. I wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sinobad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Sinobad, we'll first have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start but sometimes we have to balance the urgency of the matters that are put on our table out of court with the urgency of proceeding in court. I hope that there is some understanding for that. Mr. Sinobad, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic, and Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I please have on the screen Exhibit P2363, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, do you still have your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back in your statement to paragraph 15. You were asked some questions by the Prosecutor about this paragraph and that's the basis upon which you drew these circles. And the section marked A, you told us is the residential area mentioned in paragraph 15 where you saw shells falling; and at page 25 of today's transcript, at line 21 through 23, you were asked how many shells you saw land there, and your answer was three to four shells in A on the map. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: B, the circle, is what you have now described as the town centre. And at paragraph 15 of your statement you say you went to your office at 6.00 a.m., which was your normal time. "On the journey there, I could see that the shells were falling around the residential areas of the town and not in the town centre itself?" Do you see that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your two circles here basically cover the town of Benkovac. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So your testimony, if I understand it correctly, is that you saw four shells -- by 6.00 a.m. you saw four shells land in circle A and no shells land in circle B. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So on the town of Benkovac, by the time you started going work at 6.00 a.m., there were a total of four shells that fell on the town. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if have you any questions on this I'm going to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, I'd like to take you to paragraph -- paragraphs 18 and 19, which discuss Kolarina, your home village. You were asked at page 28 of today's transcript -- sorry, page 29 of today's transcript, whether there were any military facilities in Kolarina and you responded at line 6: "Never." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have 65 ter 1288 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a series of documents before I ask you a question, Mr. Sinobad. The first document that I am calling up is a United Nations document, and it's called, "Order of battle of the ARSK," and it identifies various units and the unit commanders and command locations. And if we scroll to the bottom of the first page in English, the third line from the bottom in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me see where that is in the -- if we scroll down a little bit in the B/C/S, please. If we can go to the next page in B/C/S, please. In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original, by the way, seems to be in French rather than in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The one rare occasion where I mistook French for English, Mr. President, but ... If we can go to the next page, please, in the B/C/S. There we go, at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, there the United Nations identifies an HQ, a headquarters, in Kolarina with precise coordinates, with a Sergeant Vasil there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in the French, please, and 3BN which is right there. If we could -- let me see ... there at the bottom in the B/C/S it says, "3 bojna." It says the locations Cista Mala and Kolarina with the coordinates, then it identifies a command structure with a Sergeant Vasil at Kolarina, with HQ Kolarina. Did you know a Sergeant Vasil in your home village there, Mr. Sinobad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there a headquarters of the ARSK in your home village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not a conscript during the war. I know Vasil as a resident of Kolarina. I don't know which post he was assigned to. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I'd like, however, to have a look at the next page in the B/C/S because I think what you just read is not for the witness ... no, I see -- yes, a little bit further up. Because in French it now reads: "Kolarina a Strazbenica," which is not entirely clear to me what is the translation of what, because you read "and."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To, I'm sorry it should have been to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that should be understand Kolarina [B/C/S spoken] should be understood as from Kolarina to Strazbenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then command in Kolarina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Command in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The original is in the French --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I'm looking at both of them and Strazbenica is where? Do we know that or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- the witness made reference to it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was a hill which was 3 kilometres south-west which is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd say it's a kilometre and a half, Mr. President, but we could check that on a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if you please pay attention so that we know exactly how to understand this evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could I have Exhibit D831, please. If we can go to page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is, Mr. Sinobad, an intelligence analysis and internal document of the 7th Knin Corps of the ARSK from February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the bottom in the English, please. Okay. Just make sure on the B/C/S -- yes. If we can go to the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just want to clarify for the transcript, Mr. Misetic had said it is a intelligence analysis and internal document of the 7th Knin Corps. I think the cover page state that it's an intelligence report from the Croatian Government and movements that were spotted. I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's intelligence assessment of the 7th Knin Corps. Mr. President, I'm interested in that paragraph at the bottom in English. I don't know why we can't find it in the ... page 6, I'm told, in the B/C/S, please. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the area of responsibility of the 3rd Infantry Brigade Benkovac, it gives you the precise locations where their line is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The line goes Ljubcen, Miranje Donje, Ceranje Donje, Pristeg, Kolarina, Strazbenica, Provic, Morpolaca. Now the question that the Presiding Judge had before I turned to this document is: What does it mean from Kolarina to Strazbenica? And what that meant was, there was a commander in charge of a specific section of the line and that line was at Kolarina to Strazbenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's not what I had that mind -- or, rather, that was not my answer. My answer was that from our positions, the positions of the army of Republika Srpska was at Strazbenica, and between Strazbenica and Kolarina there is an unpaved road. Next to it are only bushes and low trees and no settlements. That was the gist of my answer and there were no lines along that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... me. I'll just show you one other portion of this document and then we'll move on to the next one. If we go down three paragraphs to the portion that says: 3rd Battalion is deployed. The 3rd Battalion is deployed along the line Kolarina, Strazbenica, Gromile, Vuksic, et cetera. Do you know where -- having spent your whole life in Benkovac, do you know where the 3rd Battalion of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina was deployed in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was a civilian in charge of transport. I had no insight into what the positions of our army were. That was not under my competence, and I was not of that profession. It was a military matter, not a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How many trips did you take to your home village of Kolarina in 1995? How frequently would you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, every other weekend and I would spend a few hours there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you went every other weekend to the village of Kolarina and never saw military personnel in your village in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not what I had in mind. There were people there. The citizens of the village who were in uniform. They were there when they were not at the lines. At that time, basically everyone wore a uniform. In any case, I did not see them with any weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, on that point, let's turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, D156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a report that General Gotovina sent to the -- to his Main Staff on the 20th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go down to the entry at number 1. I just wanted to show you, Mr. President, that translation of ZIS, at number one, by the translation service has been -- is a -- is as a 76-millimetre gun. And if we could go to the next page, please, in English and go to line 12 in the B/C/S at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On or around 20th of July, 1995, did you notice the position of a 76-millimetre gun in the village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go, Mr. Registrar, to 1D69-0056, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm showing you now, Mr. Sinobad, is an intelligence document of the 134th Home Guards Brigade dated 31 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the report compiled at 1800 hours on that day of what was observed. The first entry says: "At 9.40 a.m., two trucks arrive from Benkovac to Kolarina. At 1045 hours, a dredge was digging between Kolarina and Perusic. At 1155, two more trucks arrived at the location where the dredge was digging, between Kolarina and Perusic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll to the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "At 1455 hours, two soldiers scouting on the trench on Mijevac, behind Kolarina, on the position with coordinates," and it gives the coordinates, "near the large trench, a yellow trench digger is conducting engineering work of the same. 30 metres to the right of the trench there is a TAM 150." Then: "Two 110s arrive from Benkovac to Kolarina." Sir, on or around the 31st of July, 1995, did you notice any trenches being dug in or around the village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1442. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have 65 ter 4522, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm now showing you the order for attack of the 134th Home Guard Regiment in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English. If we can go to page 2 in the Croatian version as well. And scrolling all the way down to the bottom in the English. And at the top in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it says the 3rd Infantry Brigade, the 3rd pb is located along the following line and it starts in the village of Kolarina. Beneath that we have where their artillery pieces are positioned. If you look at the third entry, a MB 120-millimetre platoon in the village of Kolarina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the page in English, please. And if we go to the third paragraph at the top in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it says: "The enemy is also reinforced with the armoured weaponry of the 92nd Motorised Battalion as follows." The third entry is that there are two T-34 tanks in the village of Kolarina. Now, sir, when you travelled to Kolarina in the days prior to Operation Storm or on the 4th of August itself, the first day of Operation Storm, did you notice a 120-millimetre platoon in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Particularly because on that day I failed to reach the village. As I said, I reached the initial villages -- the initial houses in the village and then turned back. I could not enter the village itself due to shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about in the days or the weekends prior to Operation Storm? Did you notice that artillery position in the village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice anything of that sort. I wasn't interested in it. I didn't notice any armoured vehicles along the way to my house or any equipment. I truly was not interested in it, and I failed to notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about these two T-34 tanks? Did you ever notice two tanks in the village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever know of any tanks in the village of Kolarina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any tanks in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1443. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1443 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could -- while this exhibit is still on the screen, if we could go to page 6 in the English. At the top. Page 4 in the Croatian, please. Okay. It's the first paragraph at the top in both English and in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says that: "The 134th Home Guard Regiment of the Croatian army shall be involved in offensive activities. Their immediate task shall be to act along the main direction of the attack carried out by the regiment, keeping under fire the Benkovac-Bribirske Mostine road and Kolarina settlement."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, would you be so kind as to get your microphone closer to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now in your statement and in your testimony again today, you mentioned meeting Major Milos Ostojic on the 4th of August as you were travelling to Kolarina. How did you -- where did you meet with Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Vigina [phoen], on the outskirts of Kolarina. There's a stretch of about 800 metres when the road starts going downwards towards the village, and that's where I encountered Major Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 1D69-0082, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an internal document of the Republic of Croatia with intelligence information from the 4th of July, 1995. And I'm interested in the paragraph that begins at the bottom of page 1 in English, and it is at page 2 in the middle of the page in Croatian. Now, concerning Mr. Ostojic, the intelligence of the Croatian authorities was that the commander of the mixed anti-armour artillery regiment is Major Milos Ostojic. Within its composition it has artillery pieces for support whose battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Commander is Lieutenant Ljubo Sekuljica. "The warehouse of the 7th Mixed Anti-Armour Regiment is located in the Slobodan Macura barracks in Benkovac." Paragraph beneath that says: "Artillery weapons of the 7th Mixed Anti-Armour Brigade are two rocket systems type Oganj, four multiple rocket launchers type Plamen, and T-12 guns which are supposedly deployed on the Kukalj range above Benkovac. The MRL type Orkan which was firing its loads from the Bijeljina village is under direct command of the corps command in Knin. Other heavy weaponry of the 7th Mixed Anti-Armour Artillery Regiment is deployed along the battlefield. I believe this morning you said that Mr. Ostojic is a relative of yours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ostojic is my wife's cousin, a distant cousin. Ostojic's mother and my wife's grandfather were brother and sister, as far as I can recall. In any case, I met him only twice in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You met him twice in your life. What was the reason that one of the two times that you met him in your life was on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was coming back from the direction of the Kolarina and when he stopped I realized it was Milos Ostojic. We had a conversation, and he advised me not to proceed because the village was under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1444.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1444 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sinobad, I have shown you a document here which indicates that someone you knew was the commander of an anti-armour artillery unit. You have seen some of the weaponry that it is alleged that he had under his command and in some of the questioning this morning you were able to indicate where artillery was not located. If I were to put a map of the Benkovac area on the screen right now for you, would be able to draw in where you believe artillery of the ARSK was located on the morning of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it seemed to me I heard the 14th, that's why I wanted to correct that. I don't think I would be able to draw that on a map. I wasn't privy to those things, I didn't know where they were and wasn't interested in either. I worked in the company and I had no information on any positions, nor were they duty-bound to inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any military training in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served my military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And were you involved at all in any artillery training when you served your military term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was with the mechanized infantry and I served in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. From my lifetime experience, I know that there are such things as mortars, multiple-rocket launchers, Howitzers, tanks, guns, but I know as much as the next person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would you able to do a crater analysis, for example, of an impact of an artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are certain differences. When less powerful pieces are used the craters are smaller, such as mortar craters. Howitzer craters are bigger, of course, depending on the charge and angle. That's why craters differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or note fire coming from the ARSK side onto the Croatian side at any time from, let's say, 1992 to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that. One could hear explosions. As for who fired shells and in what direction, I don't know. I know that such shells came from the Croatian side when they landed in the town. But as for the sounds of firing, I really can't say where they came from and who the shells were fired by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, your statement at paragraph 10, you write -- or you state that: "From 1993 to 1995, Croatian forces were shelling various Serbian towns including Benkovac and Krajina forces would retaliate but no direct contact was made in terms of an attack from either side." So is it your position that although you know that Krajina forces would retaliate, you don't know where they were retaliating from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where from. I did not leave Benkovac much and I wasn't in the area where the forces had been deployed. Therefore, I can't tell you anything with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could, on this point to 1D69-0054, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the 7th Corps command of the army of the RSK, dated 2 July 1993, issued to various commands, including the 92nd, which was in the Benkovac area. And the order states: "Lately our forces have on numerous occasions engaged in fire on civilian targets of the enemy, especially on the towns of Zadar, Sibenik, Biograd, and UN observers are located in those towns, which are immediately sending reports on our activities to their commands. Firing on the towns and civilian objectives is having a damaging effect to our reputation with the UN forces." And then he says: "With the purpose of preventing such occurrences and these particular ones, I hereby order, 1, arbitrary firing on civilian objects and towns it to be prevented and every offender held disciplinary and criminally liable. Opening fire on civilian objectives and towns shall be approved by me personally." Now, I note that in your statement you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your statement mentions that it was the RSK retaliating. Were you in fact aware that the ARSK was firing on -- sorry, arbitrarily firing on civilian objectives and towns in 1993 on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't have objections. I think that there's a mischaracterization. The order is to prevent arbitrary firing. The statement on what happened doesn't say "arbitrary" anywhere, but I don't have objections to that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections for admission. Therefore, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D1445. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1445 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sinobad, your statement, again at paragraph 10, mentions shelling of Benkovac between 1993 and 1995. My question is: Why didn't you move to Republika Srpska or Belgrade as a result of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a somewhat provocative question. Of course, the shelling in the mentioned period was sporadic, at different times and at longer intervals. That there was shelling in that period is true. We took to shelters while the shelling lasted, whereupon we would resume our normal life. At some point the bus at a bus station was hit and two high school students were killed; I don't know their names. One of the student's body parts were retrieved only a couple of days later; whereas the other student who was seeking shelter in the bus station building was hit -- was hit by the shrapnel in process. Therefore, I witnessed that particular shelling incident at the bus station. On another occasion -- well, let me tell me that my family had been present in Dalmatia for more than 200 years than was not a reason enough for me to leave the -- my century-old native place and go abroad in search of better fortunes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And that's why I'm asking you the question and why I started off my cross-examination by confirming with you that it's your position that from 5.00 a.m. to 6.00 a.m., four shells had fallen on the town of Benkovac. And in prior occasions, you say in your answer just now, that it was sporadic at different times and at longer intervals. My question again to you is: In that shelling prior to Operation Storm, why didn't -- can you tell us why you didn't decide to move your family out of the so-called RSK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not move my family out because there was no reason to. We had been living there for centuries. Let me tell you right away that I left my native area, Benkovac, only on Saturday, at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That would be Saturday, the 5th of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why did you move your family out on the 4th and 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I moved out. The entire population, due to the fire from the Croatian forces, and the possible coming in of mechanized forces, left whatever property they had and fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the reason that you and your family left was because you feared that the Croatian army would take control of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, of course, we left in an attempt to save our own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the question again is: What you were afraid of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I haven't asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I mean, if Mr. Misetic wants to finish his question, but we've had this before in mono-causal questions and that has been raised by the Chamber before and I think we have this situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's listen to the question, Mr. Misetic, you'll put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, as you can tell I have asked for one cause, and let me ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinobad, in light of the fact that you had lived through shelling of Benkovac in years prior, you didn't leave with your family on the 4th and 5th of August because of shelling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not because of shelling. Because of the danger of the Croatian forces coming in. There had been shelling in the previous years as well, but there was no danger of a direct contact with the forces, of facing the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sinobad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to turn your attention, Mr. Sinobad, to paragraph 5 of your statement -- paragraphs 4 and 5, actually, which is the planning and preparation for evacuations, and you were asked some questions about that by Mr. Hedaraly. Before I get to this new area let me ask you one follow-up question. Is it your understanding that the other people from Benkovac who left on the evening of the 4th also left not because they feared artillery but because they feared the entry of Croatian forces into Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to speak for others. Everybody have their own views and reasons for leaving, though I do believe that basically that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That was the reason -- just so that the record is clear, when you say that was the reason, you mean the threat of the entry of Croatian forces into Benkovac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, paragraphs 4 and 5 of your statement. You were shown one exhibit which you said was your plan for evacuation. And that was, I believe, D931?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, counsel? Mr. Hedaraly? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you in number 5, in paragraph number 5, you say that: "In case of danger caused by military operations, the drivers would receive their instructions regarding where to drive the civilian population from a member of the military." How would that work? Can you explain to us who in the military would tell you where to go and how the information would be relayed from the military to the actual drivers of the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plan that I was required to prepare - the request got -- came from the staff - contained the requirement for me to earmark the drivers and the locations where they were supposed to set out with the buses. Of course, I wasn't supposed to receive the information directly from them. It was supposed to go through the War Staff, and I would receive a war plan and would be required to execute it. In the particular instance I was referring to, the plan that I was supposed to draw up was meant to be implied in case of any sort of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's clarify something which I think came up in the questioning by the Prosecution. You weren't involved in the planning by the Civil Defence of evacuations of the civilian population. You were involved in planning the use of buses as part of that Civil Defence preparation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So decisions like when an evacuation would be ordered, where it would be ordered to, et cetera, that was not something that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D933, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document and see what, if anything, you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I think -- that's not the right one. D933.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6 -- sorry, e-court page 5, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If counsel plans to ask whether he has seen this document while the first page is still on before we move to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You see the title of the document is: The assessment of threats and possibilities for protection and rescue of the republican civil protection staff of the RSK. Do you recall ever seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page -- I guess at e-court page 5, page 3 of the B/C/S. It's one page before this. There we go. I'm sorry, the next page in English, please. Section 1.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to see if you know anything about any of these issues. But there's a paragraph there that says: "Due to the shape and position of the RSK which is characterized by great length, relatively small depth, vulnerability to being cut in half," et cetera. And the end of that paragraph says: "However, in the strategy of any operation, it is more likely to expect penetration of certain axes and the cutting off of parts of the territory rather than an offensive on the whole territory. In view of this, the following possibly axes of enemy attack stand out." It says: "At the northern Dalmatia operational level, possible tactical axis are the following." The first one mentioned is the Zadar-Knin axis Zadar-Benkovac-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "With the likely goal of cutting off Benkovac and Obrovac from Knin by a simultaneous attack from the slopes of Velebit and Skradin, via Bribirski Mostine with link up in the Bruska sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S, at the bottom of the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "This basis is used to assess the vulnerability of individual parts of Republika Srpska," I think it should be Republika Srpska Krajina, "which is roughly divided into three degrees." "The zone of the first degree of vulnerability includes the following."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says the second point is: "Frontier villages and towns located within ten kilometres from the present line of demarcation, villages and towns in the general area of the above mentioned tactical axes." And then the next sentence is: "Among the above, the towns of Drnis, Benkovac, Obrovac, Teslingrad, Plaski, Slunj, Petrinja, and Pakrac are especially vulnerable." Now you had, at least in some small part, something to do with plans for evacuation and my question to you is: Were you aware that the RSK authorities had found Benkovac to be in the first degree of vulnerability and that it was especially vulnerable? Was that something that was your understanding prior to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this question. Part of your job with the buses, though, and you were shown a document from 1993 by Mr. Hedaraly which was D931.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we get that on the screen, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a background question. By the 4th of August, was it your understanding that you had done everything necessary to prepare the buses in the event that an evacuation order was issued by the Civil Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Naturally, our buses were at the ready, on standby throughout the time, meaning in proper working order and filled up with fuel. They were being used on a daily basis for transportation and no additional measures needed to be issued for the preparation of these vehicles, other than they be filled up with fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Here we've seen preparations, a list of drivers, their telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That sentence right at the end. You write: "There are 100 litres of petrol in vehicles which is enough to cross 2 to 300 kilometres." On the 3rd of August, 1995, did you believe you had enough fuel to execute an evacuation, as you understood the evacuation plans to be, on the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't giving it any thought. This was the usual quantity that had to be at the disposal of the buses in order for them to run. Given the difficulties that we had in the procurement of fuel that we received through Knin, I did not give any additional request for fuel. I did not believe that there was any need for that. The situation according to all the indicators was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why, in 1993, were you taking into consideration the amount of fuel that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the minimum quantity of fuel required for the vehicles to traverse some 200 to 300 kilometres. Had the staff issued any sort of order for evacuation of the population back in 1993, on account of armed activity or any sort of natural disaster, this was deemed to be the amount of fuel required for the population to be evacuated from the Benkovac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that's the question I want to get to. How do you -- if you don't know where -- what the plans are, and you don't know where the final destination is, how do you calculate how much fuel you need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my letter, I wrote that the vehicles were filled up with 100 litres of fuel. Since I was aware of the technical characteristics of all the vehicles owned by the company, their expenditure of fuel was between 28 to close to 40 litres per --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed how many kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the amount of fuel required for them to cross as much territory, unless there was some other dire need for them to travel further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us again how many kilometres did you mention in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that 100 litres of fuel, depending on the type of vehicle, sufficed for it to cover 200 to 300 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, before the break let me ask you just a few additional questions on the issue of fuel. In paragraph 21, you talk about this meeting on the afternoon of the 4th where the evacuation was ordered and you say that: "I was further told that if there was not enough fuel for the buses at our station, that I could get fuel from the military barracks." Now, first question is: The reason that you thought there might not be enough fuel for the buses was that you were told at this meeting that you were going to Petrovac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Autotransport Company had its own in-house petrol station which was not meant for public use. Since our reservoirs were always on the minimum since it was difficult to obtain fuel from Djeletovci, Knin or whatever the location was used by the oil firm, when I was called into the staff, I was told that the final destination for the buses was supposed to be Bosanski Petrovac and that the buses, once they reached their destinations, ought to be able to return in order to evacuate all the population present in the area. We were told that the civilian population, women and children, ought to be taken to safety until the situation ends or passes. Now I don't know about all the other background information; that was up to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What military barracks contained fuel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Slobodan Macura barracks in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we take a break, Mr. Misetic, could you help me out with the D1441, that's the French document, as far as the date is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's how we got it from the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you didn't change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you used it, so you certainly will have formed an opinion about the date. I can tell you what my problem may be that. That is, I see on the fourth page out of nine, I see [French spoken] HV, 28/04/95, which could be reference to 28 April 1995. But that appears only on page 4, whereas the first page also says, [French spoken] but then it is ARSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can tell you [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's from the same date. We also see that apparently it was faxed once in August -- 27th of August, 1996, and we have an other indication for the date at -- I see something, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that it is extremely likely that it is 1995. And before Operation Storm, probably before May of 1995, because General Celeketic is identified as the commander in chief and he was replaced in May of 1995 after Operation Flash. However, this is an attachment to the witness interview or statement of Mr. Morneau who testified in this case and I believe - Mr. Hedaraly can correct me if I'm wrong - I believe he is the author or otherwise authenticated the document and I don't believe he was in Croatia prior to 1995, which would give us a rough time-frame. And the reason I tendered it is that the witness's testimony was that never was there a command in -- or a military presence in the village of Kolarina, so even if it is early 1995, it goes to the issue of how long it may have been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also see in the first page, 15/07/95, which could be a clue to July, mid-July 1995; whereas, somewhere else appears 1994, but then apparently in relation to a name. So I'm a bit lost here. Is it one document if it describes the two rather different dates, one April, one July. Is it the same document? Is it two documents? I would like to -- you would certainly assist me if you could give me further details as --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think I can, Your Honour. The statement of the witness who testified, Morneau, simply said that they were prepared by his battalion, and he attached a number of documents, that was one of them. He did not in the statement give any more information about that document. It was one of many attachments to his 1996 witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this is at least an open invitation to further assist me if anything would come to your mind in this respect. We will have a break but I would like to know what -- how much time you'd still need, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I anticipate taking the rest of the day, Mr. President, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other parties. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will probably have only a couple of questions. That means not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will try to start again at 1.00 sharp. If could you see whether the few questions of Mr. Mikulicic and what remains of the day would be sufficient, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I don't know whether you have already formed an impression about the time you might need for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It wouldn't be much up to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the parties are hereby informed that even if we would conclude with the testimony of this witness today, we would sit anyhow tomorrow in order to deal with a lot the procedural questions. Further, the Chamber needs some eight minutes itself before we finish to deliver a statement. We -- this courtroom is occupied this afternoon so we can't take -- steal time from others. Taking all this into account, I'm less pressing or urging the parties to see whether they can finish today because it might that we end up in such a hurry which is detrimental to the performance of our duties. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could please have Exhibit 1D69-0104, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a few exhibits, Mr. Sinobad. I'm quite sure you've never this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But it's a foundation for the next PowerPoint presentation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So this is a list of targets for TS -- what was then called TS-3, operative group Zadar. The list is called Jagoda and the date on the bottom of the page - if we could scroll down - is 30 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't looked at it. I don't even see it on the list that was provided to us. It may be there, but may I have a translation, if I could at least review it before stating our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is item 23 on the list that was disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot of stacionars on it, isn't it, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There are, Mr. President. Good health care in the area -- that was a joke, for the record. Item 13 in the Ring-Tail report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I will take a look at it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- is there a translation already or is there no translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because I see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, now I see it. Yes. Well, you put it first to the witness and then later, I take it, you will tender it and as long as Mr. Hedaraly has not had a look at it we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- hear from him and if need be mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D69-0145 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I will explain this to you, Mr. Sinobad, as well as to the Trial Chamber. What have you here in red, and this is from an earlier exhibit, the Court will recall, the roller coaster video that we tendered earlier of the frontline positions. This is an excerpt from that. So that line in red is the position of the ARSK on the 4th of August; and the line in blue is the position of the Croatian army on the 4th of August, and we have an overview of the wider area of Benkovac with various villages in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, according to the census map, the red is the majority Serb-populated villages, according to the 1991 census; and the blue is the majority Croat villages, according to the 1991 census. If we could go to the next page, please. Perhaps we could also have the English so that we can see the legend on the bottom. The targets on the list that I've now given to Mr. -- to the Prosecution and is briefly MFI, I hope, they have numbers that correspond to them, we've plotted the numbers according to coordinates on a wider map. The red and green are both targets on the list with the green we've -- especially identified using a colour because those are the stacionars, so that the Chamber can see where a stacionar was located. Again, the numbers next to the red dot corresponds to the line entry on the target list. If we could turn the page, please. This is just an aerial view of Benkovac. If we could turn the page again, please. These are now from the Jagoda target list in the Benkovac area and their precise locations according to coordinates. If we could turn the page, please. We have in yellow highlighted the main roads which is taken from P2327, and made them visually so that they -- the contrast is better. If we could turn the page, please. And again now we've again put the Jagoda targets over this area over the main roads and the precise locations according to the coordinates. If we could turn the page, please. And then the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is related to you. So if you could confirm for us, number 1 on this map, you see the number 1 and the line that it goes to? That number 1 is the bus station where you worked. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Number 2, is that the area of where your flat was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, the right of number 1, on the other side of the road to Obrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you -- if you were to give you a pen could you mark where you've lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Provided that this indeed is the bus station, it is in this part, in these buildings, where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember -- look at number 4, which is the police station. Do you recall that as being the location of the police station in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that's the location. Since, on this map, one would conclude that there are no more buildings behind the police station, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you draw where you believe the police station to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Before we put more markings, maybe identify with a 2 the circle where he believes his flat was before we get many circles without any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about an A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you put an A next to the first circle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now if you can draw a circle around the area where you believe the police station was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot mark the police station. I don't know what the scale is. This is far too small. I have nothing to go on, to be able to mark the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps zoom in, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We will lose the marking if we zoom in, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, are you right, Mr. Hedaraly. If we now zoom in we would -- but, of course, we could revisit it and then see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we first --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I could -- Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- store this one, because there's a possibility of storing it first and then look at the original zoom-in and then see whether we return to the stored one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, first, I think -- let me ask him a few more and see if he can mark a few more locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you -- on this map, can you find where the municipal building was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
